Why I wrote this

Everybody tells you to do strength and conditioning. Nobody tells you how.

When I started as a WNBA strength coach, I just wanted proof I was doing it right.

I searched everywhere for other WNBA strength programs to compare mine to. Nothing. The research on female athletes barely existed. The magazines weren't covering WNBA weight rooms. I was making decisions for professional athletes — Olympians, All-Stars — and I couldn't find a single resource built for women at that level.

I figured it out. And eventually, I got the validation I was looking for from the Sports Scientists with the San Antonio Spurs — one of the most respected performance organizations in professional sports. Turns out I had been doing it right all along. But I had to build that roadmap from scratch. Nobody handed it to me.

"The difference between good programs and great ones wasn't budget. It wasn't facilities. It was knowing what to do with the body in front of you. That knowledge shouldn't live only in professional locker rooms."

Search for a former WNBA strength coach creating programming for high school girls basketball coaches — you still won't find it. This guide is that resource. Everything I learned across 7 seasons, put in your hands so you're not guessing, not Googling, and not starting from scratch.

What I see in most programs

5 things that are quietly holding your athletes back

7 seasons training Olympians and All-Stars taught me what actually moves the needle for female athletes. See if any of these sound familiar.

01
Skipping the injury prevention work that actually matters for female athletes
Girls tear their ACL at 2 to 8 times the rate of male athletes in the same sport. That's not bad luck — it's anatomy. And most programs aren't addressing it at all.
02
Conditioning that doesn't match what the game actually demands
Too much focus on straight sprinting and mile times. Basketball is short explosive efforts with incomplete recovery — your conditioning should mirror that.
03
No structured lifting in-season
Two days per week minimum — even in-season. The athletes who maintain strength through a long season are the ones who finish strong in February when everyone else is running on empty.
04
Treating recovery as optional
A 2% drop in hydration causes a 10% drop in performance. Sleep drives adaptation. Your athletes are probably showing up to practice already behind — and nobody has told them why.
05
Running every player through the same program
Your point guard and your post player don't play the same game. They shouldn't train identically. You're already thinking position-specific on the floor — this guide helps you extend that into the weight room.

This guide addresses every single one.

What's inside

The things nobody ever told you about training female athletes

01
Why Female Athletes Are Different

The research has finally caught up. Female athletes aren't smaller men — they're physiologically different in ways that directly change how they should be trained. You'll understand the why for the first time.

02
The Three Tenets

The framework behind every decision I made in 7 WNBA seasons: Do No Harm → Prevent Injuries → Improve Performance. In that exact order. Most programs skip straight to number three.

03
How to Manage Your Season

Off-season, pre-season, in-season, post-season — each one has a different priority. You'll learn how to structure your year so your athletes peak when it actually counts.

04
The Game Load Protocol

In the WNBA, players over 20 minutes got a recovery session. Players under 20 got a workout. This one concept changes how you think about your athletes' bodies across a long season.

05
What a Real Session Looks Like

A complete 35-minute in-season session you can run on a practice day — prehab, compound lifts, core, and position work. Zero complicated equipment.

06
The Stuff Nobody Talks About

I once texted a WNBA player a meal plan the night before a game. Her reply: "Ok thank you so much!!" She had never been told this before. Your athletes probably haven't either.
